title: perf(comm): gather MoE-finalize routes together and accumulate in FP32
body:
## 📌 Description Stacked on #6630 (poll the local Lamport buffer); please review that one first. This makes `trtllm_moe_finalize_allreduce_fusion` faster and more accurate: - **Gather the top-k rows together.** The finalize loop handled one route at a time: load the permuted index, then load that row, then move to the next route. Each row load had to wait for its own index load. Now the kernel loads the indices and scales of 8 routes first, then all 8 rows, so the row loads are in flight together. - **Accumulate in FP32.** The routed sum, the `routed_scaling_factor`, the shared-expert add and the sum over ranks were all done in the activation dtype, rounding after every step. They now stay in FP32 and round once. This matches `allreduce_fusion` with `fp32_acc=True`. Test fixes in `test_trtllm_moe_allreduce_fusion_finalize.py`: - Its reference is now computed in FP32. The old BF16 reference does each multiply and add in BF16, and the BF16/TP4 case failed on B300 even before this change. - `scale_out` is now sized for the `SWIZZLED_128x4` layout the kernel writes: `round_up(T, 128) * round_up(H / 16, 4)` bytes. The test allocated `T * H / 16` elements, and the kernel wrote past the end. That only showed up as an illegal address once the FP32 reference allocated tensors next to it. ## 🔍 Related Issues #2269, #3671 (fused finalize slower than finalize + `kARResidualRMSNorm`) ## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist ### ✅ Pre-commit Checks - [x] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used your preferred method). - [x] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`. - [x] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues. ## 🧪 Tests - [x] Tests have been added or updated as needed. - [x] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.). B300 (SM103), TP4, CUDA 13.4. The `test_trtllm_moe_allreduce_fusion_finalize.py` row is with this PR's test file: | | before (#6630) | this PR | |---|---|---| | `test_trtllm_moe_allreduce_fusion_finalize.py` (FP16/BF16 x TP2/TP4, back-to-back) | BF16/TP4 fails | all pass (2/2 runs) | | `test_trtllm_moe_allreduce_fusion.py` | passes | passes | Latency and accuracy: one launch inside a CUDA graph, TP4, BF16, top-k 8, `launch_with_pdl=True`. Each rank has its own GEMM2 rows, softmax routing weights and shared-expert output. The reference is FP64. "stock" is FlashInfer main; "#6630" adds only the local-poll fix. | hidden | tokens | stock (us) | #6630 (us) | this PR (us) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 6144 | 1 | 8.60 | 7.50 | 6.20 | | 6144 | 4 | 8.75 | 7.63 | 6.49 | | 6144 | 16 | 9.22 | 8.25 | 7.10 | | 6144 | 32 | 15.06 | 11.14 | 9.14 | | 6144 | 64 | 26.24 | 20.13 | 15.19 | | 6144 | 128 | hangs | 38.85 | 29.02 | | 7168 | 1 | 8.80 | 8.10 | 6.56 | | 7168 | 16 | 9.66 | 8.76 | 7.40 | | 7168 | 64 | 19.08 | 13.04 | 12.11 | | 7168 | 128 | hangs | 23.47 | 21.85 | | mean abs error vs FP64 | stock / #6630 | this PR | BF16 rounding of the exact result | |---|---|---|---| | `residual_out` | 7.6e-3 to 8.0e-3 | 6.0e-3 | 4.8e-3 | | `norm_out` | 2.1e-3 to 2.2e-3 | 1.75e-3 | | End to end in vLLM (GLM-5.2-NVFP4, TP4, MTP 3, B300), with a vLLM change that finalizes each decode MoE layer in this kernel (PR to follow, it will link here). Target verify forward latency (`vllm bench forward`, CUDA graph, spread < 0.1%), deferring vs not deferring the finalize: | kernel | 1 request (4 tokens) | 3 requests (12 tokens) | 7 requests (28 tokens) | |---|---|---|---| | #6630 only | +0.4% to +0.6% | +0.4% | +2.1% to +2.2% | | this PR | -1.2% to -1.3% | -1.5% | -0.8% | That is, with only #6630 fusing the finalize does not pay off; with this PR it does. On InferenceX AgentX, GLM-5.3 vs SGLang (vllm-project/vllm#62174 with this PR, #6630 and #6632): decode time on the same turns drops 1.2-3.1% at concurrency 1-8 and 0.4% at 16 on 4x GB200, 1.6-3.1% on 4x B300.
Benchmark script: python fi_finalize_bench.py 4 out.json ```python """FlashInfer trtllm_moe_finalize_allreduce_fusion: error vs an FP64 reference and latency. usage: python fi_finalize_bench.py WORLD_SIZE OUT_JSON [--tokens 1 4 16 64 128] [--hidden 6144 7168] Each rank gets its own random GEMM2 rows, routing (top-k 8, softmax weights) and shared expert output, as in a TP MoE layer. The reference finalizes, adds the shared output, all-reduces, adds the residual and applies RMSNorm in FP64. Latency: one CUDA graph of 20 back-to-back launches, replayed 50 times, max over ranks of the median per-launch time. """ import argparse import json import socket import statistics import torch import torch.distributed as dist import torch.multiprocessing as mp import flashinfer.comm as comm TOP_K, MAX_TOKENS, EPS, RSF = 8, 2048, 1e-5, 2.5 def worker(rank, world_size, port, tokens_list, hidden_list, out_path): torch.cuda.set_device(rank) dev = torch.device("cuda", rank) dist.init_process_group("nccl", init_method=f"tcp://127.0.0.1:{port}", rank=rank, world_size=world_size, device_id=dev) results = [] for hidden in hidden_list: _, workspace = comm.trtllm_create_ipc_workspace_for_all_reduce_fusion( rank, world_size, MAX_TOKENS, hidden, group=dist.group.WORLD) for tokens in tokens_list: g = torch.Generator(device=dev).manual_seed(1000 * rank + tokens) rows = 2 * tokens * TOP_K + 8 gemm2 = (torch.randn(rows, hidden, device=dev, generator=g) * 0.5).bfloat16() idx = torch.randperm(rows, device=dev, generator=g)[: tokens * TOP_K] idx = idx.view(tokens, TOP_K).int() weights = torch.softmax(torch.randn(tokens, TOP_K, device=dev, generator=g), -1).bfloat16() shared = (torch.randn(tokens, hidden, device=dev, generator=g) * 0.5).bfloat16() gs = torch.Generator(device=dev).manual_seed(7 + tokens) # same on every rank residual = (torch.randn(tokens, hidden, device=dev, generator=gs) * 4).bfloat16() norm_w = (1 + 0.1 * torch.randn(hidden, device=dev, generator=gs)).bfloat16() norm_out = torch.empty_like(residual) res_out = torch.empty_like(residual) def run(): comm.trtllm_moe_finalize_allreduce_fusion( allreduce_in=gemm2, residual_in=residual, norm_weight=norm_w, expanded_idx_to_permuted_idx=idx, norm_out=norm_out, residual_out=res_out, quant_out=None, scale_out=None, workspace_ptrs=workspace, launch_with_pdl=True, world_rank=rank, world_size=world_size, eps=EPS, shared_expert_output=shared, expert_scale_factor=weights, routed_scaling_factor=RSF) # Every rank's workspace and inputs are ready before any rank writes to a peer. torch.cuda.synchronize() dist.barrier() run() torch.cuda.synchronize() # FP64 reference over all ranks' partial outputs. partial = (gemm2.double()[idx.long()] * weights.double()[..., None]).sum(1) * RSF partial += shared.double() dist.all_reduce(partial) ref_res = partial + residual.double() ref_norm = ref_res * torch.rsqrt(ref_res.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + EPS) ref_norm *= norm_w.double() err_res = (res_out.double() - ref_res).abs() err_norm = (norm_out.double() - ref_norm).abs() # Error of just rounding the reference to BF16, the floor for a BF16 output. floor_res = (ref_res.bfloat16().double() - ref_res).abs() s = torch.cuda.Stream() s.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream()) with torch.cuda.stream(s): for _ in range(3): run() torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(s) graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph() with torch.cuda.graph(graph): for _ in range(20): run() times = [] for _ in range(50): dist.barrier() torch.cuda.synchronize() st, en = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) st.record() graph.replay() en.record() torch.cuda.synchronize() times.append(st.elapsed_time(en) * 1000 / 20) t = torch.tensor([statistics.median(times)], device=dev) dist.all_reduce(t, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX) stats = torch.tensor([err_res.max(), err_res.mean(), err_norm.max(), err_norm.mean(), floor_res.mean()], device=dev, dtype=torch.float64) dist.all_reduce(stats, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX) row = {"hidden": hidden, "tokens": tokens, "us": round(t.item(), 2), "res_max_err": stats[0].item(), "res_mean_err": stats[1].item(), "norm_max_err": stats[2].item(), "norm_mean_err": stats[3].item(), "res_mean_err_bf16_floor": stats[4].item()} results.append(row) if rank == 0: print(json.dumps(row), flush=True) del graph if rank == 0: json.dump(results, open(out_path, "w"), indent=1) dist.barrier() dist.destroy_process_group() if __name__ == "__main__": p = argparse.ArgumentParser() p.add_argument("world_size", type=int) p.add_argument("out") p.add_argument("--tokens", type=int, nargs="+", default=[1, 4, 16, 64, 128]) p.add_argument("--hidden", type=int, nargs="+", default=[6144, 7168]) a = p.parse_args() with socket.socket() as sock: sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)) port = sock.getsockname()[1] mp.spawn(worker, args=(a.world_size, port, a.tokens, a.hidden, a.out), nprocs=a.world_size) ```

title: [Feature]: Expand MNNVL CuTe DSL AllReduce profiles beyond GB300 H=8192 TP8/TP16
body:
## Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet.

## Problem

The MNNVL CuTe DSL all-reduce fusion backend currently ships built-in static profiles only for GB300, BF16, `H=8192`, `Top-K=10`, and TP8/TP16. `MNNVLCuteDSLConfig.resolve()` keys profiles by TP size, hidden size, Top-K, and dtype, and raises `No MNNVL CuTe DSL profile supports this static shape` for other combinations.

This makes an otherwise promising backend difficult to use outside the initial Qwen3.8 2.4T-style geometry. In particular, inference engines cannot select it broadly for other tensor-parallel models or hardware without carrying custom profiles and doing their own correctness/performance tuning.

The backend's LL/BT/HT protocols cover decode through prefill and the initial implementation reports strong gains over the existing composed MNNVL and NCCL paths. Broadening the validated profile matrix would make those protocols usable by more models and would unblock a general vLLM integration instead of a model-specific one.

## Requested outcome

Expand the validated and tuned MNNVL CuTe DSL profile matrix beyond the initial GB300 `H=8192`, `Top-K=10`, TP8/TP16 configuration.

Concretely, it would be useful to have:

- Profiles for representative hidden sizes and model families beyond the initial geometry.
- TP2/TP4 coverage where the protocols and topology support it, in addition to TP8/TP16.
- Validation and tuning on SM100 and SM103, plus a clear path for architecture-specific profiles on future MNNVL systems.
- A documented/public benchmark workflow for sweeping `M`, selecting LL/BT/HT crossover points, and producing checked-in presets.
- A safe dispatch/fallback story so inference engines can probe support without hard-coding one model configuration.

## Target hardware

- SM100 (B200, GB200)
- SM103 (B300, GB300)
- Future architecture

## Inference engine

- vLLM
- PyTorch native

## Affected model or model family

Tensor-parallel models using MNNVL all-reduce fusion. The initial checked-in profiles correspond to Qwen3.8 2.4T-style `H=8192`, TP8/TP16 geometry; the request is to support additional public model shapes rather than another single-model specialization.

## Workload and configuration

- Data type and quantization: BF16 all-reduce input; fused residual add + RMSNorm, optionally preceded by MoE finalize/shared-expert add. Future quantized output fusion can be evaluated separately.
- Batch size or request concurrency: decode through prefill; sweep the full supported `M` range so LL, BT, and HT crossover points are tuned per profile.
- Sequence lengths or token counts: all; the relevant dispatch dimension is `M`.
- Parallelism: TP2/TP4/TP8/TP16 over NVLink/MNNVL, subject to topology support.
- Relevant shapes: multiple hidden sizes and Top-K values beyond `H=8192`, `Top-K=10`.
- Environment: Blackwell SM100/SM103 first; future-architecture profiles when public hardware validation is available.

## Current workaround

Use the existing TRT-LLM MNNVL, NCCL, or framework-specific all-reduce backend, or maintain a private `MNNVLCuteDSLConfig` and retune all LL/BT/HT presets and route boundaries. The first options leave performance on the table, while the latter is not a maintainable integration strategy for frameworks.

## Impact

- Missing model or hardware support
- Throughput
- Latency
- API usability or integration complexity
- Testing, maintainability, or documentation

## Acceptance criteria

- Add correctness-tested built-in profiles for at least one non-`H=8192` model geometry, and add TP2/TP4 coverage where supported.
- Exercise both fusion patterns across the newly supported profiles:
  - AllReduce + residual add + RMSNorm
  - MoE finalize + shared-expert add + AllReduce + residual add + RMSNorm
- Publish benchmark results across representative `M` values and derive LL/BT/HT route boundaries from those results.
- Preserve the existing GB300 TP8/TP16 profile performance and numerical contracts.
- Provide a support-query or documented fallback path suitable for inference-engine dispatch.
- Keep hardware-specific tuning isolated in profiles so future architectures can be added without model checks in framework integrations.

## Related work, dependencies, or suggested scope

- Initial backend: https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4358
- Related but distinct PDL-overlap request: https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/5151
- Related TP12/Kimi K3 shape request: https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/4542
- Current profile definitions: `flashinfer/comm/mnnvl_cutedsl/presets.py`
- Profile resolution: `flashinfer/comm/mnnvl_cutedsl/config.py`
- Existing routing tests: `tests/comm/test_mnnvl_cutedsl_config.py`

I can help with tuning, public benchmark sweeps, and follow-up PR work for additional shapes.

title: feat(qsa_ops): add Qwen4Exp quantized sparse attention
body:
<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->

## 📌 Description

Qwen4Exp's quantized sparse attention (QSA) for SM80 and newer, as `flashinfer.qsa_ops`, with the two pieces of common code it needs.

A QSA layer scores a compressed index cache, keeps the top blocks per query, and attends over those tokens where they sit in the paged KV cache. The package has the per-step kernels (pre-indexer, paged scorer, route expansion and mapping, output gate) and three objects that run them out of caller-owned workspaces, so a captured CUDA graph can replay a whole step: `QSASelection`, `QSAAttention` and `QSA`. `qsa_capabilities()` tells a serving stack what the build carries.

Two changes to existing code support it:

- `BlockSparseAttentionWrapper` runs on a paged KV cache (`plan(..., kv_cache_page_size=...)`; dense, FP8 or NVFP4; NHD or HND) and reports its workspace size before planning, so several live plans can share one arena. It also fixes the default FP8 scales, which were sized by the block width instead of the KV-head count.
- `top_k_ragged_transform` takes `out`, `workspace` and a resolved `backend`, so a caller can run it without allocating and with the backend fixed up front. Calls without them are unchanged.

The kernels run on SM80 and every later architecture: the JIT and AOT builds target 8.x through 12.x, and there are no architecture-specific paths, so newer GPUs run the same mma.sync and cp.async code rather than tuned variants. SM7x is excluded because the scorer's m16n8k16 arrived with SM80. The pre-indexer, scorer and route are one JIT module; the gate is a second one built without fast math, so a subnormal logistic is not flushed to zero. `cp_async.cuh` gains one L1-caching copy and `mma.cuh` the m16n8k16 helpers; existing functions are untouched.

#5859, #5860 and #5861 were folded into this PR and closed.

## 🔍 Related Issues

Tracked in #5669.

## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist

Thank you for contributing to FlashInfer! Before we review your pull request, please make sure the following items are complete.

### ✅ Pre-commit Checks

- [x] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used your preferred method).
- [x] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`.
- [x] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues.

> If you are unsure about how to set up `pre-commit`, see [the pre-commit documentation](https://pre-commit.com/).

## 🧪 Tests

- [x] Tests have been added or updated as needed.
- [ ] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.).

Each kernel is checked against a torch reference; the selection, the attention and a whole step against torch, including workspace lifetimes, plan freezing and CUDA-graph replay. The paged block-sparse route is checked against dense attention over the same entries for bf16, FP8 and NVFP4 caches, and the top-k caller-buffer path against the per-call transform. On sm_80 everything in `tests/qsa_ops`, `tests/attention/test_block_sparse.py`, `tests/utils/test_topk.py` and the trace tests passes; the SM90-only FP8 default-scale test skips. Nothing has run on SM90 or newer.

## 🔬 Experimental Track

<!-- Only for PRs submitted under the experimental policy (CONTRIBUTING.md → "Experimental APIs and Backends").
     Leave this section untouched for normal PRs. -->

- [ ] This PR is **experimental**: it adds or changes code under `flashinfer/experimental/` and/or an `@flashinfer_experimental_api`. Tracking issue: #
  - [ ] The tracking issue names an owner, the reason for the experimental path, and a graduation plan with a target release.
  - [ ] Core changes are limited to a thin entry point (signature, shared validation, feature-gate check, backend selection, handoff).
  - [ ] Tests live in `tests/experimental/` and were validated on the intended hardware; a runnable example is included.
  - [ ] Nothing is registered in `flashinfer/aot.py`, and no experimental backend is reachable from `backend="auto"` without `FLASHINFER_ALLOW_EXPERIMENTAL_AUTO_BACKENDS=1`. (Calling an `@flashinfer_experimental_api` or naming a backend explicitly is itself the opt-in and needs no environment variable.)
  - [ ] **Test scope declared below.** The experimental CI lane runs exactly these targets, so keep them as narrow as the change allows.

<!-- Required for experimental PRs. Replace the commented lines below with your targets.
     Do not delete the fence or change its `experimental-tests` tag — the experimental-track
     watcher reads it verbatim to decide which targets to ask CI for. -->

```experimental-tests
# One target per line: a directory or a file. (A pytest ::selector is not
# supported -- the sharding runner cannot consume one.) Must be under
# tests/experimental/ and must exist. Delete these comment lines and add yours, e.g.
#

#   tests/experimental/my_backend/
#
# Declaring the whole tree (tests/experimental/) is allowed but means every

```

## Reviewer Notes

The only changes to shared paths are `paged_kv_t`, which gains a `storage_page_size` field and a `resolve_slot` step on every paged kernel's address computation (a uniform branch that is a no-op when the logical block is the page), and the three keyword arguments on `top_k_ragged_transform`. Everything else is new code under `flashinfer/qsa_ops`, `include/flashinfer/attention/qsa` and `csrc/qsa_*`. The paged route is served by the FA2 kernel on every architecture; FA3 and trtllm-gen do not take a paged route here, so on SM90 and newer QSA attention runs FA2. Nothing has run on SM90 or newer.

title: [CAKE] Long-term CAKE-generated Kernel Progress Tracker
body:
To track multi-platform kernels generated from CAKE 🍰 harness + claude/codex agent. 

We are more than happy to take any new kernel challenges!

**Feel free to reach out/leave your comments/create sub-issues here to submit your customized CAKE kernel request. And we will bake it for you!**

**We know many of you have been asking for training kernels—and we heard you.** You have had your CAKE going forward; now it is time to take it **back**! Follow the dedicated forward & backward tracker at #4642, bring us your toughest training bottleneck, and let us bake the full pass together. 🍰🔥

And we recommend using agent to index the kernels you need. 😜

## Kernel categories

Pull requests are tracked in the category sub-issues below, with detailed sections and links to each PR. Please add new PRs to the corresponding category.

### Communication

Sub-issue: #6593

MoE all-reduce/finalize and residual-add/RMSNorm/combine fusion; MNNVL, Ulysses and DCP all-to-all; all-gather matmul and sequence parallelism; QKV/Norm/RoPE and MiniMax ICP exchange; FP8 GEMM + all-reduce; NVFP4-transport TP all-reduce with residual + RMSNorm fusion; Kimi-K3 TP12 tails, SM120 PCIe communication and MoK.

### Attention

Also covers fused pre-attention/output projection, QKV quantize-and-pack, QK RMSNorm/RoPE/KV append, Kimi-K3 AttnRes, and DSA indexer logits/top-k.

### Linear Attention & State Space

BF16 BMM, BF16 x FP4/NVFP4/FP8 and grouped GEMM, DeepGEMM/TinyGEMM2, all-gather matmul and router GEMM. Includes SVDQuant, runtime BF16 LoRA, per-token quantize + GEMM, projection gradients, MiniMax-H3 FC1 + SwiGLU/full-MLP fusion, and Kimi-K3 FP8 projection.

Fused MoE, AlphaMoE, MegaMoE and BGMV MoE; DeepSeek fused routing; Kimi-K3 Stable LatentMoE and fused router; warp-decode kernels.

MXFP8 quantization, fused SwiGLU + MXFP8 quantization, softmax, and RMSNorm training kernels for forward and backward passes.

Rubin/SM107 support and tuning across GDN, KDA, routing, BGMV MoE and MLA K concatenation; MiniMax-H3 SM120 shared kernels/helpers.

The seven CAKE packages (`cake_rmsnorm_train`, `cake_dsa_train`, `cake_dsa_indexer`, `cake_lm_head_loss`, `dense_projection_gemm`, `cake_moe_grouped_gemm`, `cake_mok_bf16`) build and test outside flashinfer without patches: `build.json` manifests and a shared loader, header-free bindings, behaviour switches as keyword arguments, and backend test suites that import only the package.

title: Credit each recipe's contributors on its page and in the JSON API
body:
## Summary

Each recipe page now lists the **people who wrote it**: GitHub avatars in the footer, most commits first, with links to the file's history. History links appear only for pages that have commits: the owning repo, and the old `models/` path here for recipes that moved. The JSON API carries the same list as `contributors`. The credit comes from git history, so authors fill in nothing.

### How credit is computed
`scripts/fetch-contributors.mjs` asks the GitHub GraphQL API for the commits that touched each recipe:
- in its owning repo, e.g. `vllm-project/vllm:recipes/models/…`;
- in any overlay;
- at its old `models/<hf_id>.yaml` path here, so history from before the move to vLLM still counts.

Commit authors and `Co-authored-by:` trailers count, matched to GitHub accounts by email. Not counted:
- **Bots and coding agents**, such as the `claude`, `codex` and `cursoragent` co-author trailers.
- **Commits touching more than 20 recipes**, i.e. catalog-wide maintenance like field renames, version bumps or `date_added`. The exception is the commit that created a file, which always counts, so every recipe credits its author.
- **Commits that only copy recipes between repos**: vllm-project/vllm#61302 and the `[Doc] Sync … vllm-project/recipes…` syncs. A change is credited where it was first made.

The result, `recipe-contributors.json` (hf_id → `{ contributors, history }`), is committed. A new workflow, `recipe-contributors.yml`, refreshes it every 6 hours and on `models/**` pushes, and commits any change as the bot. CONTRIBUTING has a short "Credit" section that explains the rules.

### Current data
- 215 recipes, 148 contributors; every recipe credits at least one person.
- One GraphQL run covers 401 file histories in about 40 seconds.
- Example, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: functionstackx (6), Fangzhou-Ai (5), esmeetu (4), hshrivastava-droid (4), and 10 more.

## Test plan
- [x] `node scripts/fetch-contributors.mjs` against the live API, with the results spot-checked by hand. The 6 recipes created by the YAML migration (#336) and since touched only by bulk commits now credit their author.
- [x] Local `next dev` render: a single contributor (`fishaudio/drama-3`), 14 contributors (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), and 27 contributors (Kimi-K3, all avatars shown). The "History in vllm" and "History in recipes" links appear only where those paths have commits.
- [x] `node scripts/build-recipes-api.mjs`: `contributors` appears in recipe JSON, and promoted variants inherit it the same way they inherit `source`.
- [x] `pnpm test:overlay` and `pnpm test:schema` pass.
- [ ] The workflow's first run on main, via `workflow_dispatch` after merge.

## Known limits
- Authors whose commit email isn't linked to a GitHub account aren't shown.
- History from before the YAML migration, when recipes were Markdown files in `DeepSeek/`, `Qwen/` and similar directories, isn't followed.

Summary
Enable
Engram CPU offload on H200
for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash single-node Tensor Parallel, which runs at the existing
TP4
default.
New exact-GPU
h200
override under
strategy_overrides.single_node_tp.hardware_overrides

--engram-config '{"cpu_offload":true}'
and nothing else.
A short
H200 Tensor Parallel
guide section describing the cell.
No change to the TP map.
H200 already resolves to TP4 through
tp.default: 4
, so adding an explicit
h200: 4
would be a no-op. Leaving it out also keeps this PR free of textual conflicts with
[DeepSeek] V4.1-Flash: TP2 with Engram offload on B200, B300, GB200 and GB300
#1002
, which edits that map.
Why the offload
The Engram tables are 183 GiB of the checkpoint. Row-sharded in HBM on 141 GB cards they crowd out the KV pool at TP4. Moving them to pinned host DRAM, read through UVA with unchanged output, frees 23.6 GiB per rank, 94 GiB across the replica.
Measured on the InferenceX AgentX sweep, from the c1 server log of run
35494445931
:
Quantity
Value
Engram offloaded per rank
23.6 GiB
Resident weights per GPU
81.2 GiB
KV per GPU
38.5 GiB
KV tokens (replica)
20.0M
No scheduler caps are needed at this replica size. Unlike the 180 GB B200 TP2 cell, the indexer's logits buffer fits alongside the weights with room to spare, so
--max-num-batched-tokens
and
--max-cudagraph-capture-size
stay at their upstream defaults.
Validation
InferenceX AgentX sweep green at 17 of 17 jobs, covering concurrency 1 through 128 plus evals, and the existing TP8 points re-ran green under the same config key:
SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX#3310
, run 35494445931.
node scripts/build-recipes-api.mjs
renders the H200 page at

with the Engram flag; H100 (TP8) and B300 (TP2) are unchanged.

adds TP2 with Engram offload for the Blackwell SKUs. This PR is independent: it touches only Hopper, adds its override after the
b300
block rather than before it, and makes no TP-map edit, so the two can merge in either order.

Commands use automatic pipeline discovery and specify `flow_shift: 5.0` in requests. Image builds must include the canonical `MOSSImagePipeline` registration from https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/pull/8926; the previously inspected October 14 images need that update.

- Ran the exact Base request on one RTX PRO 6000 using PR #8926 source commit `de2e050524acb638dd6590b302161e8b41c3c451`: `/health`, `/v1/models`, and `/v1/images/generations` succeeded. The inference smoke test used the source checkout; the Docker images and SFT checkpoint were not run.

title: [Perf] fuse indexer topk and page table transform fusion for dpskv4
body:
## Purpose

This PR adds a fused decode path for DeepSeek V4 C4A sparse indexer top-k and page-table index transformation. The fused kernel keeps the existing persistent_topk behavior unchanged, while adding a separate persistent_topk_with_page_table path that writes global page-table slots and top-k lengths directly during top-k output generation.

The goal is to remove the extra decode-time page-table transform kernel for eligible low-batch C4A decode cases, reducing kernel launch overhead and intermediate index processing without changing the default unfused path or prefill behavior.

Original:

```text
persistent_topk kernel
compute_global_topk_indices_and_lens kernel
```

Now:

```text
persistent_topk_with_page_table kernel
  main top-k logic
  converts local_idx -> global_slot while writing the top-k output
  writes topk_lens at the same time
```

## Test Plan
Microbenchmark

We only see performance improvements with small batch sizes and small sequence lengths.

title: [RFC]: TPSP Fusion Design
body:
### Motivation.

# RFC: TPSP Fusion Design

## 0. Goal

TPSP decomposes AllReduce into ReduceScatter (RS) + AllGather (AG), fusing RS/AG with adjacent compute (Norm, routing, GEMM) to hide communication behind computation. This brings roughly **10% TTFT improvement on long prefills**, which is especially valuable for today's agentic workloads where long-context prefill is common.


## 1. TPSP Design Principles

- **Conditionally enable TPSP based on measured performance:** A model may be compatible with TPSP without benefiting from it. Auto-profiling should identify the workload-specific crossover point, disable TPSP below it where overhead outweighs the gains, and enable it above it.
- **Enable TPSP model by model:** TPSP changes model execution structure, so models should opt in individually until the approach is sufficiently established. Models not enabled for TPSP should continue using the existing path, with no TPSP-induced change in behavior or performance.
- **Require device-side kernel support:** TPSP relies on fused kernels that may be model- and device-specific. If the required kernel is unavailable on a device, TPSP should automatically be disabled and the existing path used.
- **Share the auto-profiling framework while allowing platform-specific tuning:** Provide common profiling logic that platforms can override or extend to account for their hardware characteristics. The profiling process should complete in about 60 seconds.

---

## 2. Dense Architecture

Two fusion sites per decoder layer: **o_proj** (after attention) and **down_proj** (after MLP).

**Site A — o_proj → RS → Norm → AG**
```
            ┌────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌───────────┐
hidden ───► │ o_proj │──►│ micro-chunk   │──►│  Norm   │──►│ AllGather │──► hidden [full,H]
[full,H]    │ (GEMM) │   │ ReduceScatter │   │(+resid) │   │           │     → gate/up_proj
            └────────┘   └──────────────┘   └─────────┘   └───────────┘
```
Per micro-chunk: `GEMM → partial`, `RS(partial) → reduced`, `Norm(reduced+residual)`, `AG(norm) → full hidden`.

**Site B — down_proj → RS → (next layer's) Norm → AG**
```
            ┌───────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────┐   ┌───────────┐
hidden ───► │ down_proj │──►│ micro-chunk   │──►│ Norm (Layer L+1!)    │──►│ AllGather │──► hidden [full,H]
[full,H]    │ (GEMM)    │   │ ReduceScatter │   │ pulled forward early │   │           │     → Layer L+1 attn
            └───────────┘   └──────────────┘   └─────────────────────┘   └───────────┘
```
Layer L+1's pre-attention norm is pulled into Layer L's RS output, so AG feeds directly into the next layer with no standalone norm in between.

**Notes:** RS accumulation uses peer-visible buffers with a generation-tagged completion signal; Norm fuses "sum partials + residual + LayerNorm/RMSNorm" in one pass; chunk `m+1`'s GEMM overlaps with chunk `m`'s RS/Norm/AG. AG's physical delivery mechanism is an implementation detail, out of scope here.

---

## 3. MoE Architecture (TP MoE only)

Same two fusion sites as dense, but site ① interleaves with **routing**, and site ② interleaves with **expert permutation**.

**Site ① — o_proj → RS → Norm → Top-K/Softmax → AG + Expert Permute**
```
            ┌────────┐   ┌──────┐   ┌────────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌───────────────┐
hidden ───► │ o_proj │──►│  RS  │──►│Norm(+resid) │──►│ router  │──►│ top-k/softmax  │
[full,H]    │ (GEMM) │   │      │   │  [shard,H]  │   │ logits  │   │  (per shard)   │
            └────────┘   └──────┘   └────────────┘   └─────────┘   └───────┬───────┘
                                          │                                  │ (expert_id, weight)
                                          ▼                                  │
                                    ┌───────────┐                            │
                                    │ AllGather │◄───────────────────────────┘ (overlaps)
                                    │hidden_norm │
                                    └─────┬─────┘
                                          ▼
                                 ┌─────────────────┐
                                 │ Expert Permute    │──► grouped_hidden ──► Group GEMM
                                 └─────────────────┘
```
Routing is computed at shard granularity **before** AG, so permutation index work overlaps with the AG transfer instead of blocking on it.

**Site ② — Group GEMM → (Expert Unpermute + RS) → (next layer's) Norm → AG**
```
            ┌────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐   ┌───────────┐
grouped   ─►│ Group GEMM │──►│ Expert Unpermute + RS     │──►│ residual + Norm(L+1)  │──►│ AllGather │──► hidden [full,H]
hidden      │(per-expert │   │ (weighted sum to token   │   │   pulled forward      │   │           │     → Layer L+1
            │    FFN)    │   │ order, fused w/ cross-   │   │                       │   │           │
            │            │   │ rank reduction)          │   │                       │   │           │
            └────────────┘   └─────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘   └───────────┘
```
Unpermute and RS are **fused into one step**, not sequential: as each expert's output is scattered back to token order, it is simultaneously accumulated across ranks.

**Dense vs. MoE:**

| | Dense | MoE |
|---|---|---|
| Fusion sites | 2 | 2 (more complex) |
| Pre-AG work | none | top-k/softmax at shard granularity |
| GEMM type | standard | Group GEMM (variable per-expert batch) |
| Reordering | none | permute + unpermute (fused with RS), overlapped with comm |
| Load balancing | n/a | uneven expert load needs padding/capacity policy |

**Notes:** Group GEMM needs variable per-expert batch support; routing math stays high-precision regardless of main dtype; both sites reuse the same RS/AG signaling as dense.

---

## 4. Implementation Plan

| Stage | Goal |
|---|---|
| 1 https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60571 or https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62385 | BF16 Dense |
| 2 | BF16 MoE |
| 3 | FP8/FP4 Dense |
| 4 | FP8/FP4 MoE |
| 5 | TPSP as default modeling |

- **Stage 1/2** implement the Section 1/2 architectures as-is, on dense/MoE models respectively.
- **Stage 3** inserts Quantize just before AG on a quantized dense model, keeping RS in higher precision: `GEMM → RS (high prec) → Norm → Quantize (fp8/fp4+scale) → AG (low-bit) → next GEMM`.
- **Stage 4** layers Stage 3's quantization point onto the Stage 2 MoE pipeline using a quantized MoE model; routing stays unquantized.
- **Stage 5** makes fusion the default: unified op registration, automatic graph rewriting of `proj → AllReduce → Norm` patterns, fallback to standard AllReduce when constraints/thresholds aren't met, numerical parity tests, broader model coverage, and performance benchmarking.

### Proposed Change.

- Model Integration
- C++/CUDA operators and kernels
- Auto-profiling and tuning
- Platform backends

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Porting compiler fusions to manual fusion
body:
## Motivation.

#42770 lays out the move from full-graph `torch.compile` to manual fusion expressed directly in model code. This issue tracks the concrete porting work for **section 1-1** of that RFC: enumerating the fusions currently performed by `vllm/compilation/passes/` and mapping each one to a work item to port to a manual call site in model code. To be clear this workstream is meant to touch all existing portable model definitions where compiler fusion pass would apply previously.

The goal is **no performance regression** as we delete each compiler pass. Each fusion below is either:
- ported to a "big fused op" callable from model code,
- collapsed into another fused op,
- or explicitly dropped (with rationale).

## Proposed Change.

### Changes to QuantMethod

This is clearly needed for fusions where we are fusing the input quant op from a downstream Linear layer. When a linear layer ops in, by registering a `self.input_quant_key = QuantKey.XX`, the fused operation will return a new `QuantizedActivation` instead of a `torch.Tensor`. When the linear's kernel sees that the input is not a simple unquantized tensor, it will pass it through directly to the matmul without requantizing.

For an illustrative example for `RMSNorm + Quant` see https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42469

### Changes to Attention

TBD

### Changes to model definitions

We will initially implement these fusions for the simplest models that we can start with, and produce several subsequent PRs where we migrate groups of models to use these manual fusions, carefully testing performance and accuracy for at least one model within an architecture.

### Inventory of fusion passes

In rough priority order. Sub-issues will be filed per fused op to track ownership, kernel coverage, and the model PRs that switch over to it.

#### CUDA

- [ ] `allreduce + rms_norm[+quant]` (`AllReduceFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43499
  -  [ ] No quant
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor/per-token
  -  [ ] NVFP4
- [ ] `rms_norm[+add] + quant` (`RMSNormQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43500
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor/per-token
  -  [ ] FP8 per-token-block (1×128)
- [ ] `silu_mul + quant` (`ActivationQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43501
  -  [x] FP8 per-tensor
  -  [x] FP8 per-token-block (1×128)
  -  [x] NVFP4
- [ ] `attn + output_quant` (`AttnQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43502
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor
  -  [ ] NVFP4
- [ ] `mla_attn + output_quant` (`MLAAttnQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43498
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor
  -  [ ] FP8 per-token-block (1×128)
  -  [ ] NVFP4
- [ ] `q_norm + k_norm + rope` (`QKNormRoPEFusionPass`) - GLM4/Qwen3 / Gemma path. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43497
- [ ] `rope + kv_cache_write` (`RopeKVCacheFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43503
- [ ] `mla_rope + kv_cache_concat` (`MLARoPEKVCacheCatFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43504
- [ ] `minimax_qk_allreduce + norm` (`MiniMaxQKNormPass`)   https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43410

#### ROCm / aiter

- [ ] `allreduce + rms_norm[+add]` (`RocmAiterAllReduceFusionPass`)
- [ ] `rms_norm[+add] + (group/dynamic) fp8 quant` (`RocmAiterRMSNormQuantFusionPass`)
- [ ] `silu_mul + group fp8 quant` (`RocmAiterSiluMulFp8GroupQuantFusionPass`)
- [ ] `add + rms_norm + router_pad` (`RocmAiterTritonAddRMSNormPadFusionPass`)
- [ ] `mla_dual_rms_norm` (`MLADualRMSNormFusionPass`)

#### Compiler housekeeping (to drop, not port)

These exist only to clean up the IR and keep the compiler-fusion world consistent. With manual fusion they have no role:
- `NoOpEliminationPass`
- `VllmIRLoweringPass`
- `UnsafeCloneEliminationPass`
- `ScatterSplitReplacementPass` + `SplitCoalescingPass`
- `FixFunctionalizationPass`
- `PostCleanupPass`

These will be removed alongside the `torch.compile` integration removal (roughly the end-of-June milestone in #42770).

### Open questions.

1. **Sequence parallelism** SP today is opt-in (`pass_config.enable_sp`) and matters most for long-context + high TP. Basically it is a special case of all-reduce + rms_norm, where it turns `AR + RMSNorm[+Quant]` into `ReduceScatter + RMSNorm[+Quant] + AllGather`. We should decide whether to keep an SP path at all in the manual-fusion world.
2. **Async-TP** Not sure if this is possible to port to manual fusion.

### In-Progress.

- @mgoin tracks per-pass porting and files sub-issues from this list.
- @WoosukKwon's DSv4 NVIDIA implementation will be the reference port for P0 CUDA ops.
- @tjtanaa will handle the P0 ROCm ops.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Bugfix] Enable MLA RoPE+KV-cache fusion when layer names are hoisted
body:
## Overview

Fixes #60325.

Default `-O2` enables the existing MLA RoPE + KV-cache fusion for CUDA/ROCm MLA models when the attention layer name is a hoisted `LayerName`. The pass was off because `unified_mla_kv_cache_update` is still a Dynamo splitting op.

## Claims

- DeepSeek-V2/V3-style MLA at default `-O2` leaves `vllm::unified_mla_kv_cache_update` in the compiled piece, so `MLARoPEKVCacheCatFusionPass` can match.
- Non-MLA models and a model-less `VllmConfig()` keep today's splitting ops.
- `VLLM_USE_LAYERNAME=0`, torch older than 2.11, and platforms other than CUDA/ROCm keep the flag off.
- An explicit `fuse_rope_kvcache_cat_mla=True` that still splits the op out is disabled, with a warning.
- HiSparse with Inductor graph partition off keeps the op eager, including when HiSparseConnector turns HiSparse on after the `-O2` default.
- `use_inductor_graph_partition` stays off by default. `splitting_ops_contain_kv_cache_update()` is unchanged, so the AITER RoPE+KV default does not flip on.

## Validation

Config decisions are covered in `tests/compile/test_config.py`:

- `test_mla_rope_kvcache_fusion_splitting`: MLA + LayerName, non-MLA, plain string names, non-CUDA, no model, explicit enable with and without LayerName.
- `test_mla_fusion_follows_inductor_graph_partition`: partition on still enables the flag with no model.
- `test_mla_fusion_disabled_when_user_splits_the_op`: a user `splitting_ops` list that still contains the MLA cache op.
- `test_mla_fusion_stays_split_for_hisparse`: HiSparse set before the default, and the late HiSparseConnector case.

`ruff check` and `ruff format --check` passed on the three files with ruff 0.14.10.

The new tests were not executed in this environment. Current main does not import on the local torch 2.5.1 (`torch._inductor.custom_graph_pass` and `torch.float8_e8m0fnu` are absent; main pins torch 2.13.0).

Not run, and they need a GPU:

- `tests/compile/passes/test_mla_rope_kvcache_cat_fusion.py`
- `tests/kernels/core/test_rotary_embedding_mla_cache_fused.py`
- a DeepSeek-V2/V3 compile under default piecewise CUDA graphs, to confirm the pass matches and the cache write replays

## Details

`-O2` applies `enable_rope_kvcache_mla_fusion` before `set_splitting_ops_for_v1`. With graph partition off and `splitting_ops is None`, `splitting_ops_contain_kv_cache_update()` returns true because #33267 will append both cache-update ops. The flag stays false, and the MLA op is then split out. The fusion pattern is RoPE and that op in one piece, so it cannot match.

On torch >= 2.11, `LayerName` is a hoisted graph input, so that string constant is gone. The new branch returns true only for an MLA model on CUDA or ROCm, and `set_splitting_ops_for_v1` then skips appending `vllm::unified_mla_kv_cache_update`. `vllm::unified_kv_cache_update` is still appended.

If the pattern matches, the piece contains `fused_rope_unified_mla_kv_cache_update`. If it does not, the unfused op is still inside the piecewise CUDA graph. `use_inductor_graph_partition=True` already does that: fusion runs on the full graph, then `maybe_use_cudagraph_partition_wrapper` wraps each partition. The op reads `slot_mapping` from `BlockTable.slot_mapping.gpu`, which is filled in place before replay. That replay was not checked on a GPU here.

HiSparse's `prepare_kv_cache_update` has to run from Python every step, so the op stays a splitting op when partition is off.

`use_mla` is also true for DeepSeek-V4. V4 attention is not `MLAAttention` and does not emit this op, so the pass registers nothing and the V4 kernels are unchanged. The compile hash can change because `splitting_ops` no longer names an op V4 does not run.

This does not replace the manual fusion in #45573, and it does not close #33267. #40392's serve path (flag plus Inductor graph partition) still works through the old branch.

title: [Bugfix][Model] Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: load checkpoints with quantized q/k/v and a BF16 QSA indexer
body:
## Overview

Fixes #62308. Since #59533, `Qwen4ExpForCausalLM.packed_modules_mapping["qkv_proj"]` lists `indexer.index_qk_proj`. Quant configs read that class-level mapping before the model is built, so they check q/k/v and the QSA indexer as one fused layer. Checkpoints that quantize q/k/v but keep the indexer in BF16 fail to load with `Found different quantization schemes for the shards of ...qkv_proj`.

This PR keeps the indexer out of the mapping that quant configs see, and fuses it into `qkv_proj` only when both resolve to the same quant method.

## Claims

- Checkpoints with quantized q/k/v and a BF16 indexer load again, for example `ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-W4A16-AWQ`. Their indexer runs as its own GEMM, as before #59533.
- No change for BF16, ModelOpt FP4, and checkpoints that treat q/k/v and the indexer the same way: the indexer stays fused.
- The `--enable-lora` mapping override is removed. It is no longer needed, and it never reached the quant config.

## Validation

End to end on 4x A100-PCIE-40GB (TP4 + EP) with the `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` image built from `1b2a666` (2026-10-18). Its `model.py` and `qsa.py` match this PR's base `371745e`; for "after", the two files from this PR were mounted over them. A test-only hook (not part of this PR) logged the fusion decision of every QSA layer.

| Checkpoint | Code | Server start | QSA layers (12 per worker, 4 workers) | Check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-W4A16-AWQ` (q/k/v W4A16, indexer BF16) | before | fails: `ValueError: Found different quantization schemes ... layers.3.self_attn.qkv_proj` | - | - |
| same | after | ok | 48/48 unfused: `QKVParallelLinear` (`CompressedTensorsWNA16`) + BF16 `index_qk_proj` | GSM8K 86.2% (n=500), 0 invalid |
| `cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-AWQ-INT4` (attention BF16) | before | ok | 48/48 fused (`Qwen4ExpQSAQKVIndexerLinear`) | - |
| same | after | ok | 48/48 fused, same layer and quant method | sample request ok |

The cyankiwi "after" run used the previous revision of `_same_quant_method`, which read `scheme` only from the quant method. The final revision also reads it from the layer, which matters only when both layers are quantized.

GSM8K (an API key header was added by a small wrapper):

```bash
python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8002 --use-chat-completions \
  --model swift-1.5-flash-next-awq --reasoning-effort none --num-shots 0 \
  --num-questions 500 --max-tokens 512 --temperature 0 --max-concurrency 32
```

The default 5-shot completions mode does not suit this model family: it emits EOS right after `Answer:` once the prompt is longer than about 400 tokens, on vLLM and on llama.cpp alike.

- Unit tests (CPU): `pytest tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_quant_indexer_fusion.py`: 7 passed. With the old mapping, the two mapping tests fail with the error from #62308.
- `pre-commit run --files <changed files>`: passed.
- CI: the new tests run in the existing Qwen4 Exp step. CI has no Flash-Next checkpoint with this layout (about 165 GB), so the end-to-end load is validated only as above.

## Details

- Root cause: `configure_quant_config` passes the class-level `packed_modules_mapping` to the quant config before `__init__` runs. Even the plain `QKVParallelLinear` built before fusion is resolved as a four-shard layer. The LoRA branch rebinds the mapping on the instance, so the quant config never saw it.
- Change:
  - `packed_modules_mapping["qkv_proj"]` is `["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj"]` for both model classes.
  - `Qwen4ExpQSAAttention` builds q/k/v and the indexer as before, then fuses only if `_same_quant_method` holds: the same quant method type and the same scheme type (compressed-tensors keeps the scheme on the layer, INC on the method). Without a quant config for the fused layer (BF16, or ModelOpt FP4 via `without_modelopt_fp4`) it fuses as before.
- Limitation: if q/k/v and the indexer use the same method and scheme class but different parameters (bits or group size), they are still fused, and loading fails at weight loading. None of the 82 quantized checkpoints in #62308 has this layout.
- I used AI assistance (Claude) for the investigation, the code and the tests. I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests and GPU checks above.

title: [Roadmap] DeepSeek V4.1 Optimization
body:
Track optimization and feature support for DeepSeek V4.1 in SGLang.

## Refactor

- [x] mHC (DSV41 only) code clean up —  #42245
## General optimization

- [ ] Prefill optimizations
  - [ ] mHC SP + engram fusion — #43065
  - [x] Fold `q_rope_store` into `fused_q_norm_rope` — #41657
  - [x] Faster FP4 index-K gather and `combine_topk_swa_indices` — #41658
  - [x] Prefill indexer: raw selection, row-pair schedule IDs, and host synchronization removal — #41659
  - [x] Fused c1/c2 compression for eager extend and faster c2 decode — #41660
  - [x] Trim prefill model-entry overhead — #41704
- [ ] Decode optimizations
  - [ ] TP4 low latency attention layer #44933 
- [x] Add opt-in TRT-LLM sparse attention support — #41603 
- [ ] Integrate the MegaMoE update: locality-aware scheduling, epilogue prefetch, and shared-memory optimizations — [DeepGEMM #462](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/pull/462)
- [x] Add MegaMHC support — #42808 
- [ ] Integrate DeepEP V2.5: migrate to dedicated buffer APIs and enable the new communication optimizations — [DeepEP #763](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/pull/763)
- [ ] Packed BF16 prefill on B200/B300 — #41512
- [ ] Fuse source prefill Top-K and block maxima — #41627
- [ ] Use CUDA candidate selection in dense prefill — #40521
- [ ] Shard Engram WKV projections — #40508
- [x] Cache MXFP8 dispatch — #42156
- [ ] Persist FlashInfer autotune measurement policies with cached tactics — #42158
- [x] Reduce eager Engram extend preparation — #42159
- [ ] Replace the legacy topk-v2 with DeepSelect (need LL optimization) — #44051 

## Feature: bounded replay

Goal: both replay flags on by default — same accuracy, never slower than off, faster prefill.

### Encoder replay

- [x] Fix SWA page size with bounded replay — #42128
- [x] Bounded replay with sparse mla - #42273 
- [ ] Enable encoder bounded replay.
  - [x] Fold the replay into the extend forward (16 × 64K hits: 4.6 s → 1.0 s TTFT) — #43166, #43165
  - [ ] Cut decode request-window copies (+6–11 ms → +0.3 ms per step) — #42715
  - [ ] Cut prefill request-window overhead (cold prefill gap 26% → 2%) — #42921
  - [ ] Serve HiCache host-tier hits — #42716
  - [x] Keep the DSpark draft SWA from cutting prefix hits — #44673

### Decoder replay and prefill graph

- [ ] Enable decoder bounded replay.
  - [x] Serve prompt-logprob requests under decoder replay — #44850
  - [ ] Enable the prefill CUDA graph by default for DeepSeek-V4.1 (+19% cold prefill) — #43440 
  - [ ] Make both replay flags compatible with the prefill graph
  - [ ] Capture eager prefill layers as graphs (+54% cold prefill)
  - [ ] Lift the 16K prefill-graph cap; faster prefill all-reduce

### Compatibility and default

- [ ] Support decoder SWA bounded replay with prefill CP and static DSpark PD — #40161
- [ ] DP attention and PD disaggregation
- [ ] Turn both replay flags on by default

## Feature: PD

Original roadmap: #39700 (B200).

### Prefill

- [ ] Support context parallelism — #40323
- [ ] Support CP with breakable CUDA graphs — #40333
- [ ] Avoid host synchronization in CP prefill — #40335
- [ ] Support CP with multistream forward preparation — #40179
- [ ] Reuse shared compressed KV dequantization — #40421
- [ ] Fuse candidate selection and masking — #40436
- [ ] Capture indexer and compressor in breakable CUDA graphs — #40548

### Decode

- [x] Support DP attention — #40177
- [ ] Support MegaMoE — #40178

## Hopper optimization

- [x] Optimize dense GEMM, indexer, mHC, and MoE paths on Hopper — #41251
- [ ] Support candidate-only SM90 indexer scoring — #40860
- [ ] Skip invisible SM90 FP4 indexer tiles — #40503
- [ ] Add an FP8 Tensor Core path for the FP4 grouped indexer — #40160
- [ ] Use DeepSelect Top-K with fused page mapping for Hopper decode — #41561
- [ ] Enable Hopper decode optimizations for TP8 — #39114
- [ ] Add H20 block-FP8 tuned configurations — #41098
- [ ] Add and extend H200 block-FP8 tuned configurations — #40452

title: [NVIDIA] DeepSeek V4 Perf Tracking
body:
## Motivation

This follows [DeepSeek V4 Roadmap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/23602), which covers functional enablement; this issue is perf-only.

**Scope**: NVIDIA SM90 / SM10X.

---

## High priority

- [x] Integrate TRT-LLM DSv4 attention for SM100/103 #30805
- [x] FlashInfer MNNVL backend for pure (non-fused) allreduce #30700
- [ ] Overlap scheduling for online C128 MTP #30497
- [ ] Split mixed-chunk attention: route decode tokens to the fp8 paged MLA kernel #30338
- [x] Emit TMA-aligned UE8M0 scales for the FP8 einsum #34277

title: [Perf] Optimize DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Hopper paths and Blackwell prefill selection
body:
## Motivation

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Hopper spends substantial decode time in group32 dense GEMMs, capacity-sized indexer work, mHC statistics, and padded Marlin MoE projections. This PR tunes those paths. On Blackwell, flattened prefill selection also launches separate mask, sort, slot-map and raw-offset operations; the added integer kernel combines them.

## Changes

- Tune Hopper group32 GEMMs and reuse exact BF16 expansions of eligible FP8 weights, preserving activation quantization boundaries and the original fallbacks.
- Use live paged indexer lengths and variable-length top-k; fuse masking, sorting and slot mapping.
- Enable guarded Hopper mHC combine/norm and compensated BF16 projection paths, with decode statistics overlap.
- Preserve intermediate activation rounding in fused clipped SwiGLU; defer MXFP4 padding until Marlin repacking.
- On SM100-family CUDA GPUs, fuse flattened prefill selection into one integer kernel. Keep the changing visible slot count as a non-specialized runtime argument, so new context lengths do not create new JIT variants. Hopper retains its existing Torch selection path.

## Pinned validation

Checkpoint `dba1be0a40aa45a94ad051997016db3960a90277`; PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130 and sgl-kernel 0.4.8; sgl-bench commit `a9da34ad1f997ca05878d858d3d01970e4a49af9`; sgl-eval 0.1.2. Both machines were allocated exclusively for these comparisons. All paired datasets, request counts, input/output lengths and API errors were validated from the request records. Timings exclude profiling and correctness instrumentation.

### H200: upstream main versus original PR runtime

8×H200, TP8/EP1, Marlin MoE, static memory fraction 0.8, bounded SWA replay, decode graph maximum batch64, Engram host table disabled. Main `ef867fa40d` versus PR `22e352d873`; `94d21e3162` differs from the measured PR only by a test mock accessor. Random8192 input /1024 output, seed42, temperature0, thinking disabled,64 warmup requests and cache flush. Request counts30/40/80/80/160/320 at concurrency1/4/8/16/32/64; three alternating paired sweeps. Ratios below are medians of the three paired ratios.

|Concurrency|User-speed ratio|Output-throughput/GPU ratio|TTFT speedup|
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|1|2.2067×|2.1515×|1.3398×|
|4|2.4842×|2.3498×|1.5062×|
|8|2.3599×|2.2322×|1.5551×|
|16|2.1674×|2.0574×|1.5555×|
|32|2.2540×|2.1077×|1.5658×|
|64|2.3975×|2.1929×|1.5583×|

The final Blackwell addition was checked separately against the original PR on the same H200 node: one complete paired six-point sweep and full GSM8K/AIME24 at4096/32768 output caps. User-speed ratios are0.9990–1.0029 and output-throughput/GPU ratios0.9989–1.0013. This additional check is one paired sweep, not the three-sweep main comparison above. Full GSM8K is1277/1319 on both arms; AIME24 is456/480→457/480, with23 truncations each. Hopper continues to use its Torch fallback; equal aggregate scores do not imply identical generations.

### GB300: added flattened prefill fusion versus ordinary PR

4×NVIDIA GB300/SM103, ARM64, TP4/EP1, flashinfer_mxfp4 MoE and flashinfer_cutedsl FP8 GEMM. Ordinary PR `94d21e3162` versus candidate `179b1ab2d3` (identical tested file hashes). Both arms use16384 for chunked-prefill-size and max-prefill-tokens. Three rotated paired sweeps; seed42, temperature0, thinking disabled,16 warmups and cache flush. Each shape uses64 requests at concurrency1 and128 at concurrency16.

|Input tokens|Output tokens|Concurrency|Median TTFT speedup|Individual paired ratios|
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
|8192|32|1|1.0170×|1.0227×, 1.0170×, 0.9902×|
|8192|32|16|1.0277×|1.0266×, 1.0485×, 1.0277×|
|32768|32|1|1.0209×|1.0209×, 1.0282×, 0.9794×|
|32768|32|16|1.0200×|1.0200×, 1.0239×, 1.0168×|

Both concurrency16 shapes improve in all three pairs. Each concurrency1 shape has one regressing pair, so this is a small prefill improvement, not a claim of universal or statistically proven acceleration. In the8192-input/1024-output suite, median output-throughput/GPU ratios are only1.0009–1.0081. The standalone selection helper improves5.45–14.33×; that microbenchmark is not an end-to-end speedup.

### Accuracy

Full GSM8K1319 problems, thinking disabled; full AIME24 is30 problems×16 repeats, thinking enabled. Seed42, temperature0,32 evaluation threads, no API errors. Repeats are not480 independent questions. Results are paired by question ID, problem text and expected answer.

|Machine|Dataset/output cap|Upstream main|Ordinary PR|Blackwell candidate|
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
|H200|GSM8K/2048|1278/1319|1278/1319|Not rerun at this cap|
|H200|AIME24/16384|440/480|437/480|Not rerun at this cap|
|H200|GSM8K/4096|1276/1319|1274/1319|See fresh paired run below|
|H200|AIME24/32768|451/480|454/480|See fresh paired run below|
|H200, fresh paired run|GSM8K/4096|Not rerun|1277/1319|1277/1319|
|H200, fresh paired run|AIME24/32768|Not rerun|456/480|457/480|
|GB300|GSM8K/2048|1277/1319|1278/1319|1279/1319|
|GB300|AIME24/16384|438/480|437/480|434/480|
|GB300, fresh paired run|GSM8K/4096|Not rerun|1279/1319|1277/1319|
|GB300, fresh paired run|AIME24/32768|Not rerun|456/480|453/480|

GB300 accuracy uses2048 prefill budgets, because upstream main's FlashMLA scheduling metadata exceeds its48KB shared-memory implementation limit on a GSM8K batch at the default16K budget. Performance comparisons use the same16K budget on every arm and are kept separate. AIME24 candidate versus ordinary PR changes by−0.625 percentage points; truncations40→42,14 correct→wrong and11 wrong→correct. There is also one additional wrong nontruncated answer. The higher-cap paired run still has AIME24 −0.625 percentage points (456→453 correct; truncations22→24;7 correct→wrong,4 reverse), and GSM8K −0.1516 percentage points (1279→1277; neither arm truncated). These scores do not prove identical generation or statistical accuracy equivalence.

### Correctness coverage

- Existing H200 focused regression:582 passed,60 skipped,16 subtests passed on the rebased runtime.
- New integer selection/CUDA Graph/cache-reuse cases:34 passed on real GB300 SM100 dispatch, and34 passed on H200 with the SM100 entry mocked to exercise the integer helper.
- Full GB300 indexer test file:133 passed,2 skipped.
- Real-model8K/32K prefill audit at concurrency1/16:1908 calls across four ranks, with both page and raw indices exactly equal to the original Torch operations. Rows1–16384, visible slots1–48900. This is integer-mapping evidence, not a substitute for generation-quality evaluation.
- A second actual-model audit dispatches fusion before any reference GPU work:1908 calls,477 per rank, with exact page/raw index agreement. Padding is separately covered by the unit tests.
- Actual model GPU traces contain40 `_finish_flat_indexer_topk_kernel` events per rank; all four original trace files are retained with source hashes.
- Pinned pre-commit and diff whitespace checks passed. CI is not fully green: the existing AMD raw-draft-metadata test still needs alignment with main's deferred metadata API; no ROCm validation is claimed.

## Memory and weight updates

The Hopper derived caches trade GPU memory for throughput. In the original weight-load measurement, memory increased72.71→75.43GB/GPU and max_total_num_tokens fell16,012,800→14,223,104 at the same static memory fraction. These are the original configuration's measurements, not newly measured final-commit memory numbers.

Online weight updates require disabling both derived caches with `SGLANG_OPT_HOPPER_BLOCK_FP8_BF16=0` and `SGLANG_OPT_DEEPGEMM_HC_PRENORM=0`; otherwise updates fail before writing weights. Other TP/EP layouts are not covered by the reported serving comparisons.

Single-node H20-3e report: vision CP + DSpark, long-prefill improvements, and three upstream PRs
Thanks for maintaining this roadmap and for the kernel/CP work behind it. We have been integrating and testing DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on
one 8× NVIDIA H20-3e server
, with text, image+text, tool calling, streaming, and cache reporting as requirements.
Our October 5–7 experiments started from
unmodified SGLang v0.5.21
and ended with a production deployment of a pinned integration build. The strongest paired comparisons were:
524,032-token cold TTFT: 323.261 → 25.531 s
, a
92.1% reduction / 12.66× speedup
.
C64 aggregate output: 877.01 → 2,534.61 token/s (+189.0%)
; per-request streaming decode:
15.69 → 49.10 token/s (+213.0%)
.
These are
whole-deployment improvements
, not the isolated effect of any one PR. We have contributed
#39306
,
#42922
, and
#42924
; their narrower validation and attribution are described below.
1. Setup and measurement scope
Hardware: 8× H20-3e, SM90, approximately 140 GiB visible memory per GPU, NVLink/NVSwitch (NV18 topology), 2 TiB host RAM, two NUMA nodes.
Baseline: v0.5.21 at
e00930c5489053f26d86b179cee0d087f846acbb
,
TP8/EP8, DSpark block size 5 already enabled
, no CP, no decoder bounded replay, GPU-resident Engram, no HiCache.
Final:
TP8/EP4, CP8 interleave, CP decode-attention TP, DSpark5, decoder SWA bounded replay
, FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE with FP8 precision; Engram host table in
per_rank
layout, NUMA binding, HiCache ratio 1.5 /
write_through
.
Both use a 524,288-token context limit, static memory fraction 0.8, chunk size 8192 and max-running-requests 64. Prefill CUDA graphs remain disabled; decode CUDA graphs are enabled.
Final local integration revision:
79b468a7435e1bd29ad0d377587ff10b3c214ba3
(
not an upstream release/commit
). Runtime: PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, Triton 3.7.1, FlashInfer 0.6.18; the final DeepGEMM integration uses
sgl-deep-gemm 0.2.2
. This is a backported integration, not a claim that stock v0.5.21 supports this configuration.
The baseline and final integration use the same V4.1 model weights on the same hardware. No P/D disaggregation is used. All performance below is from a single eight-GPU server. These results describe the pinned October 5–7 snapshots, not the latest heads of every roadmap PR.
Comparison boundary:
the near-512K and C64 baseline measurements were supplemented using exactly the final workload construction, warmup and three measured rounds. Input hashes, token counts, output lengths and zero-cache-hit conditions match. Other baseline cells are historical references: cold-prefill nonces differ, and the early natural-generation prompts/warmup procedure differ from the final protocol. The tables explicitly mark the paired supplements with †. Runs were sequential, on different dates, not randomized interleaved A/B trials.
2. Optimization path and what we retained
Use vision-compatible CP as the foundation.
We chose
model: DeepSeek V4.1 vision CP and single-owner image encoding
#40219
for its merge-before-shard multimodal preparation and single-owner image encoding. We adapted the owner callback API and fixed physical request-pool row mapping in the Torch prefill indexer. We borrowed the replay-tail idea from
[DSV4.1] DeepSeek-V4.1 support prefill CP

Integrate the Hopper paths and H20 configurations.

[DSV4.1] Add H20 block-FP8 tuned configs

per_rank

title: Odds-Shift Slippage in One-vs-Rest Rankers: Diagnosing and Repairing Reweighting-Induced Top-K Errors
body: One-vs-rest rankers that show each user the top-$K$ of many rare labels usually counter imbalance with a per-label positive-class weight, scale_pos_weight $= n_-/n_+$. Elkan's identity says such a weight shifts label $j$'s log-odds by $\ln w_j$, so the model ranks by weighted odds rather than by the marginal that is Bayes-optimal for precision@$K$, and suggests inverting the shift afterwards; what a finite learner does with a weight in the thousands, and which repair then works, has not been measured. We call the gap between the promised and the realized shift odds-shift slippage and measure it on matched pairs of LightGBM and MLP models that differ only in the weights. On Santander the weight takes MAP@7 from 0.808 to 0.117; for the boosted pairs the ideal odds shift accounts for 23% of that loss (32% on Instacart; 98% for an MLP pair on the same rows) and slippage for the rest. We prove that a booster whose leaf steps are capped at $c$ realizes at most $Tηc$ nat of shift in $T$ rounds at rate $η$, which a cap sweep confirms, and show that without a cap saturated cells tie at exactly 1.0, beyond the reach of any separable map. The analytic inversion therefore pays only where the shift was realized and nothing saturated, whereas per-label isotonic regression returns the Santander model to 0.784 (0.780 with the calibrator fitted on the validation period), but only if labels without calibration positives are mapped to their prior rather than passed through. On 11 public MULAN benchmarks and 5 learners the weighted model loses more than half of its MAP@$K$ in 8 of 55 cells, and on delicious and Corel5k the same repair returns it to the unweighted level; per-label calibration hurts where positives are scarce, a harm that a cross-validated rule removes. The recipe is released as oddslip.

title: Magnifying What Matters: Attention-Guided Adaptive Rendering for Visual Text Comprehension
body: Visual Text Comprehension (VTC) renders text into images for a vision-language model (VLM) to read, sidestepping LLM context-window limits and powering applications from long-page OCR to multi-page memory QA. Yet existing VTC pipelines treat rendering and layout as a fixed, content-agnostic preprocessing step and offer little mechanistic understanding of how VLMs internally process visualized text. Through a focused empirical study on VTC QA tasks, we reveal that VLMs exhibit a localization-without-utilization regime: evidence-localizing attention emerges sharply in the middle-to-late layers and is largely decoupled from answer correctness, yet simply enlarging the localized spans on the rendered page recovers a large fraction of the failures. Building on these observations, we propose AGAR (Attention-Guided Adaptive Rendering), a training-free, model-agnostic method that leverages a VLM's own middle-to-late layer attention to identify the top-K important visual patches, maps them back to word spans, and re-renders the page with those spans enlarged before re-inferring the answer. Extensive experiments across nine VTC benchmarks (short-form, long-context, and multi-page memory QA) and four VLM backbones show that AGAR (i)consistently improves off-the-shelf VLMs as a plug-and-play enhancement, (ii)composes with VLM post-training to yield further gains, and (iii)remains robust under both visual- and text-side input degradation.

title: Certifiably Robust Interpretation via Renyi Differential Privacy
body: Motivated by the recent discovery that the interpretation maps of CNNs could easily be manipulated by adversarial attacks against network interpretability, we study the problem of interpretation robustness from a new perspective of \Renyi differential privacy (RDP). The advantages of our Renyi-Robust-Smooth (RDP-based interpretation method) are three-folds. First, it can offer provable and certifiable top-$k$ robustness. That is, the top-$k$ important attributions of the interpretation map are provably robust under any input perturbation with bounded $\ell_d$-norm (for any $d\geq 1$, including $d = \infty$). Second, our proposed method offers $\sim10\%$ better experimental robustness than existing approaches in terms of the top-$k$ attributions. Remarkably, the accuracy of Renyi-Robust-Smooth also outperforms existing approaches. Third, our method can provide a smooth tradeoff between robustness and computational efficiency. Experimentally, its top-$k$ attributions are {\em twice} more robust than existing approaches when the computational resources are highly constrained.

title: LangGS-SLAM: Real-Time Language-Feature Gaussian Splatting SLAM
body: In this paper, we propose a RGB-D SLAM system that reconstructs a language-aligned dense feature field while sustaining low-latency tracking and mapping. First, we introduce a Top-K Rendering pipeline, a high-throughput and semantic-distortion-free method for efficiently rendering high-dimensional feature maps. To address the resulting semantic-geometric discrepancy and mitigate the memory consumption, we further design a multi-criteria map management strategy that prunes redundant or inconsistent Gaussians while preserving scene integrity. Finally, a hybrid field optimization framework jointly refines the geometric and semantic fields under real-time constraints by decoupling their optimization frequencies according to field characteristics. The proposed system achieves superior geometric fidelity compared to geometric-only baselines and comparable semantic fidelity to offline approaches while operating at 15 FPS. Our results demonstrate that online SLAM with dense, uncompressed language-aligned feature fields is both feasible and effective, bridging the gap between 3D perception and language-based reasoning.

title: Kitty: Accurate and Efficient 2-bit KV Cache Quantization with Dynamic Channel-wise Precision Boost
body: The KV cache is a dominant memory bottleneck for LLM inference. While 4-bit KV quantization preserves accuracy, 2-bit often degrades it, especially on long-context reasoning. We close this gap via an algorithm-system co-design for mixed-precision KV caching: Kitty. On the algorithm side, extensive experiments show that Dynamic Channel-wise Precision Boost -- which ranks Key-cache channels by sensitivity and keeps only a small fraction at higher precision -- maintains near-zero loss in accuracy drop while approaching 2-bit memory. The main challenge is handling dynamic 4-bit channel boosts while keeping the page layout coalesced and the dequantization uniform, with no scattered reads or hard-coded masks. Kitty addresses these issues by decompose each mixed-precision Key page into two tensors with unified 2-bit precision. Based on this, Kitty provides a page-centric KV layout, Triton-compatible page dequantization kernels, and a lightweight runtime pipeline that preserves coalescing and avoids divergence. Across seven tasks and two model families (Qwen3, LLaMA3), Kitty cuts KV memory by nearly 8x with negligible accuracy loss, enabling up to 8x larger batches and 2.1x-4.1x higher throughput under the same memory budget. We release the full implementation of Kitty at https://github.com/Summer-Summer/Kitty.

title: AerialFusionMapNet: Online HD Map Construction with Aerial-Onboard BEV Fusion
body: High-resolution aerial imagery has recently emerged as a complementary modality for automated driving perception and has shown potential to improve birds-eye-view (BEV) scene understanding when fused with onboard sensors. Prior work demonstrated performance gains for online high-definition (HD) map construction through aerial-onboard fusion; however, conventional end-to-end fusion does not fully exploit the structural information contained in aerial representations. In this work, we introduce AerialFusionMapNet, a fusion-based mapping framework with a structured two-stage training strategy that explicitly enhances the contribution of aerial features within a unified pipeline. The proposed training scheme enables more effective integration of structural aerial priors. On the nuScenes geographic split, AerialFusionMapNet achieves up to 54.7 mAP, improving over prior aerial-onboard fusion baselines from 48.8 mAP by +5.9 absolute and +12.1% relative. The results suggest that structured training design, rather than increased architectural complexity, plays a more decisive role in unlocking the full potential of aerial imagery for online HD map construction. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/DriverlessMobility/AerialFusionMapNet.

* config(dsv41flash): change the MI355X memory split only where KV ran short

The previous commit applied one memory split per TP across every
concurrency. Concurrency 1-32 never ran short of KV, so it paid for
changes it did not need: offloaded Engram lookups go to pinned host
memory over UVA, and a smaller prefill chunk costs TTFT. Scope each
change to the points that were actually starved, which also leaves
concurrency 1-32 and TP=4 c64 byte-identical to the settings run
35574132719 already measured on this image and flag set, so those
points are combined with this sweep rather than re-run.

Dividing measured KV tokens by concurrency gives the per-request budget
and separates the failures cleanly. Every point that held had 232K or
more; TP=2 c64 collapsed at 122K.

  TP=4 c1-c64   resident, 16384   14.83M tokens   232K and up
  TP=4 c128     offload,   8192   49.63M           388K
  TP=2 c1-c32   offload,  16384    7.84M           245K and up
  TP=2 c64      offload,   8192   24.68M           386K
  TP=2 c128     offload,   4096   33.34M           260K

Probing the configurations directly also turned up two things. TP=2 c128
at 4096 with the API-server default of 1024 sequences faults during
profiling with HSA_STATUS_ERROR_EXCEPTION at M=1024, N=129280, K=256,
reproduced on two GPU pairs: DSpark verifies 1+5 tokens per sequence, so
a decode batch of max_num_seqs needs six times that many token slots and
4096 leaves four. Cap max_num_seqs at the graph-capture shape wherever
the chunk falls below that bound, which is TP=2 c128 alone. And the
reason c128 never completed before is that at 16384 with capture at
2048, TP=2 c128 held 7.72 GiB, 3.02M tokens, 23.6K per request.

* refactor(minimaxm3-atom): one table per concurrency, and drop the tier M3 cannot use

The hybrid offload tier is unreachable for this model. ATOM's M3 connector is
PAGE-only -- the docstring says MiniMax-M3 has no recurrent state and no SLOT
sidecar, and it raises if slot_regions is non-empty -- so OFFLOAD_STATE and the
staging knobs behind STATE_OFFLOAD_CPU_GIB never applied. Its LMCACHE_CHUNK_SIZE
is justified by "block-size(128) x dcp(8)", but this model's search space sets
no dcp-size at all. Removed, along with the comment claiming M3 carries a
per-request recurrent state. An unlisted concurrency now fails instead of
silently taking a tier that does not fit.

CONC=56 is removed for the same reason: nothing in the matrix runs it here (the
56 in this file's neighbourhood belongs to Kimi K3, which has its own script),
and it was the only band that disabled the draft model. With it gone
NUM_SPEC_TOKENS is constant, so the guard around SPEC_ARGS goes too.

The remaining per-concurrency facts now live in one table. Previously the CP
gate was a numeric comparison and the offload tier an enumeration, so adding a
concurrency above 24 would silently enable indexer CP on a point nobody
measured, while forgetting the tier failed loudly. Both are declared per band
now: the loud failure is kept, the silent one becomes a missing speedup.

Verified the same way as the previous cleanup: all 19 matrix points replayed
through a stubbed benchmark_lib, server argv and every exported env var
byte-identical.

* perf(minimaxm3-atom): extend indexer CP down to CONC=15 on TP4

The gate was CONC > 24, chosen from a kernel microbenchmark over uniform
contexts. Three same-commit A/B pairs (1800 s per arm, TP4 + EAGLE3) put the
real crossover below 15:

  CONC 15   interactivity p90 +3.7%    ISL-normalised throughput +0.67%
  CONC 24                    +12.3%                              +0.24%
  CONC 28                    +16.7%                              +2.7%

Monotone and never negative. Throughput is neutral everywhere (only CONC=28
clears the 0.6% noise floor) while interactivity rises with the running batch,
which is what CP actually shortens. Prefix hit rates are identical within each
pair (96.7/96.7, 97.5/97.5, 97.2/97.3), so the gain is not a caching artifact.

CONC=20 is interpolated between the two measured points, not run on its own.
Nothing below 15 is measured and the microbenchmark is negative at batch ~2,
so the band stops there.

CONC=20 appears in both search-space rows, so it is split out of the offload
enumeration: TP4 gets CP without a tier, and the tp_size == 4 gate keeps CP off
the TP2 offload curve. 25 and 30 are TP2-only and stay without a CP
declaration, which would never take effect but would misreport the point.

Verified with the 19-point argv+env replay: the only difference against the
previous revision is ATOM_M3_INDEXER_CP="1" on tp4_c15, tp4_c20 and tp4_c24.
